blocks.text: The heading places Amos’s setting during the overlapping reigns of Uzziah of Judah and Jeroboam son of Joash of Israel, a setting in the middle of the eighth century BCE. It identifies Amos as being among the herdsmen of Tekoa, but does not supply the fuller biography sometimes imagined for him. Neither this description nor related occupational terms securely establishes whether he was poor, wealthy, or what his precise livelihood was.

The remembered earthquake in verse 1 functions as a chronological marker, but the text itself gives no exact year, magnitude, epicenter, or identifiable destruction layer. Proposed correlations remain uncertain, so the reference should not be treated as a precise historical date.

sections.title: The Earthquake as a Time Marker

blocks.text: The judgments against Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, and Ammon use the repeated formula, “for three transgressions, yea, for four.” This is a way of presenting offense as accumulated and full, not a literal count of exactly four crimes. The sequence continues beyond this chapter through further nations and leads toward an indictment of Israel; claims about how an original audience may have reacted to the earlier judgments remain reconstruction rather than certainty.

The charges are not general statements about the character of whole peoples. They name acts such as wartime brutality, the carrying away and delivery of captives, broken kinship obligations, and relentless violence. The passage’s judgments therefore should not be used to assign collective ethnic guilt to modern groups.
